etymology: Hebrew ’alwah, “evil” or “moral perverseness,” also written Aliah, a duke of Edom named among the chiefs that came of Esau in mount Seir.
biblical_def: Alvah is named among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau according to their families and their dwelling-places (Gen 36:40). The sacred record sets him in that register of the line of Esau, of whom it is written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). The dukes ruled the land which the LORD had given unto Esau for a possession, for He said to Israel of the children of Esau, “I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession” (Deu 2:5). Yet over all this dominion stood the ancient word of the oracle, that the elder should serve the younger, for the LORD had said, “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.” The dictionary does not labour to recover the deeds of Alvah, of whom Scripture tells us only his name and his office; it honours that the Spirit of God thought it good to write him in the book. Edom rose to chiefs and habitations before there reigned any king in Israel, but its glory was earthly and its end was judgment, as Obadiah foretold. Alvah stands as a witness that even the proud dukedoms of Esau are numbered and bounded by the God who keeps the times and the bounds of every nation’s habitation.

etymology: Hebrew yetheth, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “a nail” or “subjection,” a duke of Edom named among the chiefs that came of Esau.
biblical_def: Jetheth is named among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau according to their families, after their places, by their names (Gen 36:40). He belongs to that register which the Spirit of God appended to the line of Esau, of whom it stands written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). These dukes held dominion in the land the LORD had granted to the children of Esau, for He charged Israel, “Meddle not with them… because I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession” (Deu 2:5). The Horims dwelt there beforetime, but the children of Esau succeeded them and dwelt in their stead (Deu 2:12). Of Jetheth himself the Scripture records nothing beyond his name and his office; the dictionary does not invent a history where God has given only a name. Yet the bare naming is no idle thing, for it shows that the LORD took knowledge of Edom’s chiefs even as He governed the line of promise in Jacob. Edom flourished in dukes and habitations, but pride lifted up its heart (Oba 1:3), and the word of the LORD by the prophet was a word of cutting off. Jetheth stands among the names of a nation that gloried in its strength and forgot the God who gave it.

etymology: Hebrew ’oholibamah, “tent of the high place,” here a duke of Edom, bearing the name of Esau’s wife Aholibamah, daughter of Anah.
biblical_def: Aholibamah is reckoned among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau (Gen 36:41), and bears the name of Esau’s wife Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah, who was of the Horite stock of the land (Gen 36:25). The name itself, “tent of the high place,” carries an echo of the worship of the heights, for Edom was a land where the LORD was not feared. This duke belongs to the register set down after the line of Esau, of whom it is written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). The dukes held the land the LORD had given Esau for a possession (Deu 2:5), succeeding the Horims who dwelt in Seir beforetime (Deu 2:12). The dictionary does not seek to distinguish every motion of so obscure a chief; it sets down faithfully that the Spirit of God numbered Aholibamah among Edom’s dukes. The name borne first by a wife and then by a duke shows how the houses of Esau intermarried with the people of the land and took root in mount Seir. Yet root and dukedom alike came under the prophet’s word of judgment, for the LORD purposed against the inhabitants to make their habitations desolate (Jer 49:20). Aholibamah stands among the names of a nation whose tents and high places were appointed to fall.

etymology: Hebrew ’elah, “an oak” or “terebinth,” here a duke of Edom, the name distinct from King Elah of Israel and from the valley of Elah.
biblical_def: Elah is named among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau (Gen 36:41). The name signifies “an oak” or “terebinth,” a strong and rooted tree, and it is borne elsewhere in Scripture by other men: by Elah king of Israel, son of Baasha, who reigned but two years and was slain in his drunkenness (1Ki 16:8-10), and the valley of Elah is that vale where David smote Goliath the Philistine. This Elah, however, is none of these, but a chief of Edom, set in the register appended to the line of Esau, of whom it is written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). He held his place in the land the LORD gave unto Esau for a possession (Deu 2:5). The dictionary distinguishes the dukes of Edom from the kings of Israel that the reader confound them not, and honours that the Spirit named even this obscure chief. The oak speaks of an earthly strength that seems to abide; yet Edom’s strength was vanity, for the LORD had pronounced its wisdom perished and its men dismayed (Jer 49:7). Elah stands among the rooted chiefs of a nation whose oaks the LORD purposed to fell, that the mount of Esau might be cut off by slaughter (Oba 1:9).

etymology: Hebrew pinon, “darkness” or perhaps “a region of mines,” a duke of Edom named among the chiefs that came of Esau.
biblical_def: Pinon is reckoned among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau (Gen 36:41). The name has been understood to signify “darkness,” and some have joined it to a place of mines and pits in the land of Edom, where in later ages men dug for copper. He belongs to the register appended to the line of Esau, of whom Scripture saith, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). The dukes ruled in the land the LORD had given Esau for a possession, having succeeded the Horims who dwelt in Seir beforetime (Deu 2:12). The dictionary records Pinon as it stands, neither adding to his history nor subtracting from it, for the Spirit of God gave us his name and his office and no more. Yet the very meaning of the name, if it be “darkness,” suits the land it adorned, for Edom dwelt without the light of the covenant and the worship of the true God. The LORD stretched out His hand upon Edom, to make it desolate from Teman (Eze 25:13). Pinon stands among the names of a people in darkness, a witness against all dominion that is gotten and held apart from the LORD, the Father of lights.

etymology: Hebrew qenaz, “hunter” or “possession,” here a duke of Edom, distinct from Kenaz the Kenizzite and the kindred of Caleb.
biblical_def: Kenaz is named among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau (Gen 36:42). The name is borne by more than one man in Scripture, for there was Kenaz a grandson of Esau and son of Eliphaz (Gen 36:11), and from a Kenaz came the Kenizzites and the line of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, and Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, the first judge of Israel (Jdg 3:9). This duke is to be distinguished from these, being a chief of Edom set in the register appended to the line of Esau, of whom it is written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). He held his place in the land the LORD had given unto Esau for a possession (Deu 2:5). The dictionary keeps these Kenazes apart that the reader err not, marking that one name may stand in two lines, the one of Edom and the one that married into the people of God through Caleb. Edom and Israel sprang of the same father Isaac, yet the elder served the younger by the ancient word. Kenaz of Edom stands among the chiefs of a rejected line, a witness that the LORD chooseth whom He will, and that grace, not blood, maketh the heir of promise.

etymology: Hebrew teman, “the south” or “the right hand,” here a duke of Edom, his name also borne by the region of Teman renowned for its wise men.
biblical_def: Teman is named among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau (Gen 36:42). The name signifies “the south” and was given also to a son of Eliphaz, Esau’s eldest, and to the region of Teman in Edom, a country renowned for the wisdom of its men. It was of Teman that the prophet asked in the LORD’s name, “Is wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished?” (Jer 49:7); and from this country came Eliphaz the Temanite, the first of Job’s three friends. This duke belongs to the register appended to the line of Esau, of whom it stands written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). The dictionary honours the renown of Teman’s wisdom, yet marks that earthly wisdom, however celebrated, perisheth before the LORD. For all its prudent men, Teman was appointed to dismay, that every one of the mount of Esau might be cut off (Oba 1:9), and the LORD purposed to make its habitations desolate (Jer 49:20). Teman stands among the names of a people wise in their own conceit, a witness that the fear of the LORD, not the counsel of the prudent, is the beginning of wisdom.

etymology: Hebrew mibtsar, “a fortress” or “a stronghold,” here a duke of Edom named among the chiefs that came of Esau.
biblical_def: Mibzar is named among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau (Gen 36:42). The name signifies “a fortress” or “a stronghold,” and it suits the land of Edom well, for Esau dwelt among the clefts of the rock and the high places of mount Seir, trusting in the strength of his mountains. He belongs to the register appended to the line of Esau, of whom it is written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8). The dukes held the land the LORD had given Esau for a possession (Deu 2:5). The dictionary records Mibzar as the Spirit gave him, a name and an office and no more; it does not feign a history. Yet the meaning of the name preacheth its own sermon, for Edom said in its heart, who shall bring me down to the ground? — trusting in its strongholds as if no power could reach them. But the LORD declared that though Edom exalt itself as the eagle and set its nest among the stars, thence would He bring it down (Oba 1:4). Mibzar, the fortress-name, stands among the chiefs of a people that trusted in the strength of rock and height, a witness that no stronghold is sure but the LORD, who is the only fortress of His people.

corruption_paragraphs: Mibzar is a name of the Edomite register, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name among the dukes of Esau may know it for a real chief in a real land of strongholds in mount Seir.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD alone is the true fortress of His people. Edom trusted in the strength of its rocks and the height of its dwellings, and said in its heart that none could bring it down; yet the LORD declared He would cast it from the stars. The believer flees not to the strongholds of his own making, but to the name of the LORD, which is a strong tower, into which the righteous runneth and is safe.

etymology: Hebrew magdi’el, “preciousness of God” or “prince of God,” here a duke of Edom, the last but one named among the chiefs of Esau.
biblical_def: Magdiel is named among the dukes of Edom, the chiefs that came of Esau, set near the close of the register with duke Iram (Gen 36:43). The name carries within it the syllable for God, signifying “preciousness of God” or “prince of God,” a striking thing to find among the chiefs of a people that knew not the LORD in covenant. He belongs to the line of Esau, of whom it is written, “Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom” (Gen 36:8), and the dukes are reckoned according to their habitations in the land of their possession, “he is Esau the father of the Edomites” (Gen 36:43). The land was given them of the LORD, for He said, “I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession” (Deu 2:5). The dictionary records Magdiel as the Spirit gave him, a name and an office and no more. Yet the name preacheth, for a man may bear the name of God upon his lips and in his very title and yet dwell in a land appointed to judgment. Edom had outward greatness, dukes and habitations and the name of God woven into its chiefs, but it lacked the fear and worship of the LORD. Magdiel stands as a witness that an empty profession of the divine name, without the heart that fears Him, cannot turn aside the judgment of God.

etymology: Hebrew lotan, “covering” or “a wrapping,” the son of Seir the Horite, a duke of the Horites, father of Hori and Hemam and brother of Timna.
biblical_def: Lotan was a son of Seir the Horite, of the people who inhabited the land of mount Seir before the children of Esau (Gen 36:20). He is reckoned among the dukes of the Horites: “duke Lotan, duke Shobal, duke Zibeon, duke Anah” (Gen 36:29). His children were Hori and Hemam, also called Homam, and his sister was Timna (Gen 36:22), the same Timna who became concubine to Eliphaz the son of Esau and bare Amalek. Thus the Horite stock of Lotan was joined by marriage into the house of Esau, and the children of Esau succeeded the Horims and dwelt in their stead (Deu 2:12), for the LORD had given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession (Deu 2:5). The dictionary records Lotan as a chief of the older inhabitants of Seir, marking how the LORD removeth one people and planteth another according to His purpose. The Horims were a real people, dispossessed in their season, even as the Edomites who came after them were appointed to judgment in their own. Lotan stands at the head of a list of vanished chiefs, a witness that the LORD ruleth in the bounds of every habitation, raising up and casting down the dwellers of the earth, and that no people holdeth its land but by His leave and for His appointed time.

The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name among the sons of Seir may know it for a real chief of a real people who dwelt in mount Seir before the Edomites.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the bounds of the nations. He hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Act 17:26). The Horims dwelt in Seir beforetime, and the children of Esau succeeded them; and Esau in turn came under judgment. No people holdeth its land save by the leave of the LORD and for His appointed season; the believer learns to hold all earthly dwelling loosely, as a pilgrim toward a city that cannot be moved.
